title: Parse a fixed-width payroll extract
prompt:
A mainframe payroll job writes one line per employee, with no delimiters between fields — every field sits at a fixed character position:

| field | start (0-based) | length |
|---|---|---|
| id | 0 | 6 |
| name | 6 | 20 |
| salary | 26 | 10 |
| dept | 36 | 3 |

`name` is space-padded on the right to fill its width. `salary` is zero-padded on the left and always has exactly two decimal digits, for example `0004250.00`. Lines are separated by `\n`, and the file may contain blank lines.

Return an array of `{ id, name, salary, dept }`, one per non-blank line, with `name` and `dept` trimmed and `salary` as a Number.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
hints: The payload here is one big String with newlines in it, not a parsed structure — there is no reader doing the work for you. Split it into lines first.

Each field lives at a fixed character position, not behind a delimiter. A range selector like line[6 to 25] on a String pulls out a substring; pair every field with trim, since the padding is real characters, not formatting.

Describe the layout as a list of { name, start, length } and reduce over it per line. Two things bite: a field width that is off by one silently drops or adds a character instead of erroring (it only shows up when a value exactly fills its column), and a blank line in the file is not a record — filter it out before parsing, or it survives the split and fails later at the `as Number` coercion instead of at the split.

explanation.approach: There is no reader for this format here — application/flatfile in this engine requires a schema resource loaded from the classpath, and passing one inline as a reader property does not satisfy it (it fails with 'No schema set' no matter what the property is named). So the file arrives as inputMime text/plain, a single String, and the parsing is manual: split on newlines, then pull each field out of a line with a range selector at a fixed offset. The two ways this goes wrong without an error are a field width that is off by one, and a blank line that survives the split.

snippets.label: The payload is a plain String here, not a parsed structure
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload splitBy "\n"
snippets.note: splitBy on the raw text gives an array of line Strings. Nothing has been parsed into fields yet.

snippets.label: A range selector plus trim pulls one field out
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
trim("E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[6 to 25])
snippets.note: line[6 to 25] is the 20-character name column, spaces and all. trim removes the padding — it does not know or care where the padding came from.

snippets.label: A parsed field is still a String until you say otherwise
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  raw: "E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35],
  rawType: typeOf("E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35]),
  asNumber: "E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35] as Number
}
snippets.note: The salary column comes out as the String "0004250.00". as Number drops the leading zeros and keeps the cents — 4250, not a display string.

snippets.label: Why application/flatfile is not the answer here
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
read(payload, "application/flatfile", {schema: [ {name: "name", size: 10}, {name: "age", size: 3} ]})
snippets.note: This is the built-in flat-file reader, and it looks like the right tool. It throws IllegalStateException: No schema set regardless of what the schema property is called or shaped — this engine expects the schema as a classpath resource, which a headless practice script has no way to supply. Range selectors on a String are the fallback that actually works.

snippets.label: One column short is silent, not an error
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var layout = [ { name: "name", start: 6, length: 19 } ]
fun field(line, start, length) = trim(line[start to (start + length - 1)])
---
field("E00002Bartholomew Chen III0001500.75SAL", 6, 19)
snippets.note: r2's name is exactly 20 characters — "Bartholomew Chen III" — with no padding to spare. Reading only 19 of them drops the trailing "I" and returns a different, still-plausible-looking name. No exception, no null — just a wrong answer, and only on the one row with no slack in it.

snippets.label: A blank line fails later than you'd expect
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
("" splitBy "\n") map (line) -> line[26 to 35] as Number
snippets.note: An empty line has no character at position 26 — the selector returns null, and null as Number throws UnsupportedTypeCoercionException. The failure surfaces at the coercion, several steps after the split that actually produced the bad element, which is why filtering blank lines up front is easier than debugging this backward.

title: Send an XML document inside a JSON envelope
examObjective: Converting between output types and data types using DataWeave
basics: `write(value, "application/xml")` turns a value into XML text, a String, which can then be placed inside a JSON field like any other String. A third argument passes writer properties, such as `{ indent: false, writeDeclaration: false }`, which control how the text is laid out.
prompt:
A logistics partner accepts orders as JSON, but the order itself must be an XML document in a String field:

```
{ "ref": "O-1", "xml": "<order><id>O-1</id><line>A</line></order>" }
```

The payload is `{ id, lines }`, where `lines` is an array of SKUs. Build the envelope with `ref` set to the id, and `xml` holding an `order` element with one `id` and one `line` element per SKU, written on one line with no XML declaration.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
hints: `write` returns a String. Build the XML structure as an Object with a single root key, then write it.
An Array under a key becomes repeated elements with that key.
Pass `{ indent: false, writeDeclaration: false }` as the third argument of `write`. Then try an order with no lines: an empty Array still writes an element, so make the field conditional.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  ref: payload.id,
  xml: write({ order: { id: payload.id, (line: payload.lines) if (!isEmpty(payload.lines)) } }, "application/xml", { indent: false, writeDeclaration: false })
}

explanation.approach: Embedding one format in another means serialising the inner document to a String first, which is what `write` does. The value written has to be a valid XML shape, with a single root, and the writer properties go in the third argument. The hidden trap is the empty order: an empty Array under `line` does not vanish, it becomes one empty `<line/>`, so the field has to be left out when there are no lines.

snippets.label: write returns text
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
typeOf(write({ order: { id: 1 } }, "application/xml"))
snippets.note: In the JSON output, it is an ordinary String field.

snippets.label: The default layout
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
write({ order: { id: 1 } }, "application/xml")
snippets.note: A declaration and line breaks, unless you turn them off.

snippets.label: An empty Array is not nothing
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
write({ order: { line: [] } }, "application/xml", { indent: false, writeDeclaration: false })
snippets.note: One empty element, which the partner reads as a line with no SKU.

snippets.label: Two roots
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
write({ id: 1, lines: [] }, "application/xml")
snippets.note: An XML document needs exactly one root element.

snippets.label: An Array becomes repeated elements
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
write({ order: { line: ["A", "B"] } }, "application/xml", { indent: false, writeDeclaration: false })
snippets.note: One element per value.

title: Embed an order's line items as a CSV attachment
prompt:
Each order is `{ orderId, items }`, where `items` is an array of `{ sku, qty, price }`.

Return an array of `{ orderId, csv, total }`:

- `csv` is the order's line items written out as CSV text, with columns in the order `sku, qty, price` — a String, embedded as one field of the JSON output, not a separate file.
- `total` must be computed by reading that same CSV string back and summing `qty * price` over its rows — not computed straight from `items`.

An order with no items has `csv` as an empty string and `total` of `0`.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
hints: `write(value, "application/csv")` does not print anything — it returns a String. Put that String straight into a field of the object you output, the same as any other value.

The columns `write` produces follow the field order of the objects you hand it, not any order tied to the question. If an item's own JSON has `price` before `sku`, writing that item as-is puts `price` first in the CSV too — rebuild each row as `{ sku: ..., qty: ..., price: ... }` before writing, so the column order is yours, not the input's.

`read(csv, "application/csv")` gets you back an array of objects, but every field on them is a String, `qty` and `price` included — the numbers you wrote in are not the numbers you read back. Coerce with `as Number` again before multiplying.

explanation.approach: `write(value, mime)` is a function like any other: it does not print, it returns a String holding the rendered CSV, ready to sit inside a field of a JSON object the same as a number or another string would. The first surprise is that this is exactly right — the CSV shows up in the output as one long string with `\r\n` escapes in it rather than looking like a table, because a JSON string cannot contain a literal newline. The second surprise is where the column order comes from: `write` uses the field order of the objects it is given, not any order implied by the question, so an item that arrives with `price` before `sku` writes `price` first unless each row is rebuilt with the field order fixed by hand before writing. The third is that `read` undoes the format but not the types — everything that comes back out of a CSV is a String, including the numbers, so they need `as Number` again before they can be multiplied.

snippets.label: write returns a String; embedded, it is an escaped blob
snippets.note: typeOf confirms it is just a String. Sitting inside the envelope it shows up as `\r\n`, not real line breaks — that is what a JSON string does to any text with newlines in it, and it is exactly what should happen here.

snippets.label: column order follows the object's own field order, not the question's
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
write([{price: 3, sku: "F6", qty: 4}], "application/csv")
snippets.note: This row's own JSON lists price, then sku, then qty, and the CSV header comes out in that same order — price first. Nothing about `write` knows the columns are supposed to read sku, qty, price.

snippets.label: the fix is rebuilding the row before writing it
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var raw = {price: 3, sku: "F6", qty: 4}
---
write([{ sku: raw.sku, qty: raw.qty, price: raw.price }], "application/csv")
snippets.note: Same data, rebuilt as `{ sku, qty, price }` first. The column order is now the one the object literal states, not whatever order the source happened to arrive in.

snippets.label: read reverses the format but not the types
snippets.note: The 2 and the 9.5 went in as Numbers and came back as the Strings "2" and "9.5". read does not remember what the values were before write turned them into text.

snippets.label: the total needs those fields coerced back to Number
snippets.note: Without `as Number` on both fields, this multiplies Strings that only look numeric, which is not the computation the question asks for even on the rows where it happens not to throw.

title: Run a list of pricing rules through a pipeline
prompt:
Each order has a `base` price and a `rules` array. Each rule is `{ op, amount }`, where `op` is `"add"`, `"mul"`, or `"sub"`. Starting from `base`, apply the rules **in the order given** — an `"add"` adds `amount`, `"mul"` multiplies by `amount`, `"sub"` subtracts `amount`. An `op` that is none of those three leaves the running total unchanged.

Return an array of `{ id, total }`. An order with no rules keeps its `base` as `total`.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
hints: A rule is naturally a one-argument function from price to price: give the operation and amount, get back a function that does that step. That is partial application — a function returning a function.

`then` composes a value with a callback — `then(x, f)` is `f(x)`. Fold the rules array into a chain of these with `reduce`, seeding the accumulator with `base` the way `[] reduce ((i, acc = 0) -> acc + i)` seeds it with `0`.

The natural first draft, `acc then applyOp(r.op, r.amount)`, does not compile — the infix form of `then` only accepts a literal lambda on its right, not a call to a named function. Write it as `then(acc, applyOp(r.op, r.amount))` instead, and never as separate running totals grouped by operation: `add`s and `mul`s do not commute, so grouping them loses the order the rules were given in.

explanation.approach: A rule is a step in a pipeline, and the natural way to represent a step is a one-argument function: give `applyOp` the operation and amount, and it hands back a function from price to price without running it yet — that is partial application. `then` is DataWeave's way to compose a value with a callback: `then(x, f)` is exactly `f(x)`, and folding the rules array with `reduce`, calling `then` once per rule, builds the pipeline in the order the rules appear. The trap is that `then` has two faces. Its function-call form, `then(acc, applyOp(...))`, accepts any callback, including one that came from calling a named function. Its infix form, `acc then applyOp(...)`, does not — it only works when the right-hand side is a lambda written out inline, and fails the moment it is a call to a `fun`, whether or not that call still takes more arguments. The two forms are not interchangeable despite looking like the same operation written two ways.

snippets.label: Partial application: a function that returns a function
snippets.note: applyOp("add", 5) does not compute a number — it returns a Function, still waiting for `x`. Calling that result with (10) is what actually runs the addition.

snippets.label: then's function-call form composes it
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun applyOp(op: String, amount: Number) = (x: Number) -> op match {
  case "add" -> x + amount
  case "mul" -> x * amount
  else -> x
}
---
then(10, applyOp("add", 5))
snippets.note: then(10, applyOp("add", 5)) is then(10, f) where f is the function from the previous snippet — it runs f(10) and gets 15. This is the form the pipeline is built from.

snippets.label: The infix spelling of the exact same thing does not compile
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun applyOp(op: String, amount: Number) = (x: Number) -> op match {
  case "add" -> x + amount
  case "mul" -> x * amount
  else -> x
}
---
10 then applyOp("add", 5)
snippets.note: Same values, same callback, written as `10 then applyOp("add", 5)` instead of `then(10, applyOp("add", 5))`. It fails with UnsupportedTypeCoercionException: Cannot coerce Function to String. Infix `then` does not accept a callback produced by calling a named function — bare or applied, with or without type annotations, it fails the same way. This is why the pipeline has to be built with the function-call form, not the infix one.

snippets.label: Infix then is fine with a lambda written out inline
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
10 then ((x) -> x + 5)
snippets.note: The only difference from the previous snippet is that the callback here is a lambda literal instead of a call to `applyOp`. It compiles and runs. `then` itself is not broken — only its infix form's tolerance for where the callback comes from is limited.

snippets.label: Order changes the answer, which is why grouping by operation is wrong
snippets.note: Same two rules, opposite order, different totals — 220 against 210. An approach that sums all the adds and multiplies by all the muls as separate batches cannot tell these two apart, because it throws away the order the rules came in.

title: Salvage the good meter readings from a bad batch
prompt:
A batch of raw meter readings arrives as `{ id, value }`, where `value` is a String that is supposed to represent a number but sometimes is not — empty, `null`, or text.

Return `{ ok, failed }`: `ok` is an array of `{ id, value }` for every reading whose `value` coerces to a Number, with `value` as that Number; `failed` is an array of just the `id`s whose `value` does not coerce. One bad reading must not stop the rest of the batch from being processed.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
hints: Coercing a bad String with `as Number` throws — it does not return null or a sentinel value. Left alone, that exception unwinds the whole script, not just the one record it happened on.

`dw::Runtime` has a `try` function: `try(() -> someExpression)` runs the expression and comes back with `{ success: true, result }` or `{ success: false, error }` instead of throwing. Wrap the risky coercion in a zero-argument lambda and pass it to `try`.

Checking `value != null` and `!isEmpty(value)` first does not help — a String like `"abc"` is neither null nor empty, and `as Number` throws on it anyway. The only thing that actually contains the failure is running the coercion inside `try` and branching on `.success`.

explanation.approach: `as Number` on a bad String does not return `null` or fail quietly — it throws, and by default that exception propagates out of the whole script, not just out of the one record that caused it. `dw::Runtime` has `try(() -> expr)`, a function that runs a zero-argument lambda and catches whatever it throws, coming back with `{ success: true, result }` or `{ success: false, error }` either way. Wrapping just the risky coercion in `try` — not the whole record, and not a hand-rolled null/empty check first — is what lets the rest of the batch keep going.

snippets.label: try on a coercion that succeeds
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::Runtime
output application/json
---
{ success: try(() -> "12.5" as Number).success, result: try(() -> "12.5" as Number).result }
snippets.note: try never throws itself. On success it hands back the result under `.result`, alongside `success: true`.

snippets.label: try on a coercion that fails
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::Runtime
output application/json
---
{ success: try(() -> "abc" as Number).success, kind: try(() -> "abc" as Number).error.kind, message: try(() -> "abc" as Number).error.message }
snippets.note: The same exception that would otherwise abort the script shows up as data under `.error`, and `success` is `false` instead of the script halting.

snippets.label: without try, one bad row aborts the whole array
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map (r) -> { id: r.id, value: r.value as Number }
snippets.note: M1 and M3 are perfectly good readings, but M2 alone is enough to throw the whole map expression, and with it the whole output. There is no partial result.

snippets.label: null coerces no better than a bad string
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::Runtime
output application/json
---
{ success: try(() -> null as Number).success, kind: try(() -> null as Number).error.kind, message: try(() -> null as Number).error.message }
snippets.note: A missing value is just another way this throws, with a different exception kind. `try` catches it the same way, with no special-casing needed for null.

snippets.label: checking for null and empty first does not prevent the throw
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---

title: Rename every key, everywhere, at any depth
prompt:
You are given JSON of unknown shape — objects nested inside arrays nested inside objects, to any depth. Every key that uses `snake_case` has to come out `camelCase`, no matter how deep it sits.

Only keys change. A value is left exactly as it is, even if it happens to be a string that itself looks like `snake_case` — `"account_status": "in_progress"` becomes `"accountStatus": "in_progress"`, not `"accountStatus": "inProgress"`.

The input is not always an object at the top. It can be an array, and arrays can hold plain scalars as well as objects — a list of tags, for instance, sitting next to a list of line items.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
hints: You don't know the depth or the shape ahead of time, so this can't be a fixed chain of selectors — it needs something that looks at whatever it's handed, and calls itself again on whatever's inside.

Write it as one function with three branches: an Object recurses into its values while renaming its own keys, an Array recurses into its elements, and anything else — a String, a Number, `null` — is returned as-is. Nothing in core loops for you; the branching by type is what does the walking.

`dw::util::Tree`'s `mapLeafValues` looks tailor-made for a generic walk, but check what it actually touches before reaching for it: it rewrites the leaf VALUES, not the keys along the way, so it does not do this job. And when your Array branch hits an element, don't assume that element is an Object — `special_tags` is an array of plain strings, and calling an object-only function on one of those is what breaks a first attempt that otherwise looks right.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun camelKey(s) = do {
  var parts = s splitBy "_"
  var rest = parts[1 to -1] default []
  ---
  parts[0] ++ ((rest map ((w) -> upper(w[0] default "") ++ (w[1 to -1] default ""))) joinBy "")
}
fun rewrite(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> o mapObject ((val, key) -> { (camelKey(key)): rewrite(val) })
  case a is Array -> a map rewrite($)
  else -> v
}
---
rewrite(payload)

explanation.approach: There is no built-in that walks arbitrary JSON and renames keys — the shape isn't known until you're looking at the value in front of you, so the walk has to be written as a recursive function with one branch per kind of value: an Object renames its own keys with `mapObject` and recurses into each value; an Array just recurses into each element, unchanged in kind; anything else (`String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `null`) is a leaf and comes back untouched. `dw::util::Tree`'s `mapLeafValues` looks like it should help — it also walks a whole structure — but it transforms leaf VALUES, and this task is about KEYS, so it doesn't apply here. The part that actually catches people is the Array branch: it's tempting to assume every array holds more objects, but an array can just as easily hold scalars, and calling an object-only function on a scalar element is a hard error, not a smaller correct answer.

title: Strip empty fields from a payload at every depth
examObjective: Defining, using, and reusing DataWeave modules, functions, and variables
basics: A recursive function that walks any JSON value usually has three cases: an Object (process each field and recurse into its value), an Array (recurse into each element) and anything else (return it as it is). `match` with `is Object` and `is Array` picks the case.
prompt:
A partner API rejects requests that contain empty fields. Before sending, remove every **object field** whose value is `null` or the empty String `""`, at any depth, including inside objects that sit in arrays.

Arrays keep all their elements, even null or empty ones: only object fields are removed.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
hints: `filterObject` at the top level passes the sample. The hidden payloads nest the empty fields.
Write a function that handles an Object, an Array and a plain value, and calls itself for the first two.
For an Object: filter the fields, then `mapObject` each remaining value through the function. For an Array: `map` each element through it, without filtering.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun strip(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> o filterObject ((x) -> x != null and x != "") mapObject ((x, k) -> { (k): strip(x) })
  case a is Array -> a map strip($)
  else -> v
}
---
strip(payload)

explanation.approach: Only object fields are removed, so the function filters inside Objects and never inside Arrays, but it still has to recurse through Arrays to reach the Objects inside them. `skipNullOn="objects"` on the writer comes close, removing null fields at every depth, but it knows nothing about empty Strings.

snippets.label: The writer option
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json skipNullOn="objects"
---
{ a: null, b: "", c: [null, { d: null }] }
snippets.note: Null fields go at every depth. The empty String stays.

snippets.label: The recursive function

  case o is Object -> o filterObject ((x) -> x != null and x != "") mapObject ((x, k) -> { (k): strip(x) })
  case a is Array -> a map strip($)
  else -> v
}
---
strip({ a: null, b: "", c: [null, { d: "", e: 1 }] })

title: Fix it: strip empty fields from a payload at every depth
basics: A recursive function that walks any JSON value usually has three cases: an Object (process each field and recurse into its value), an Array (recurse into each element) and anything else (return it as it is). `match` with `is Object` and `is Array` picks the case.
prompt:

title: Nested orders out as flat CSV rows
prompt:
Each order in the input is `{ order_id, customer, line_items }`, where `line_items` is an array of `{ sku, qty, price }`.

Produce a CSV with one row per line item — `orderId, customer, sku, qty, price` — where `orderId` and `customer` are repeated on every row that came from that order. An order with no line items contributes no rows at all. A line item missing a field leaves that cell empty rather than failing the row.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
---
hints: The output has more rows than the input has orders — each order can expand into several rows, or none. That's a shape where you map over the outer list, then map again over something inside each element, and merge the two levels of results back into one flat list.

`flatMap` is `map` followed by one level of flattening in a single step: the outer function returns an array of rows for each order, and `flatMap` concatenates all of those arrays into one. An order with an empty `line_items` array returns an empty array of rows, which contributes nothing — which is exactly the behavior the empty-order case needs, for free.

Name the outer order in the lambda — `(order) -> ...` — and read `order.order_id` and `order.customer` from that name inside the inner map, not from `$`. Inside a nested `map`, `$` always means the innermost element, the line item, so `$.order_id` there is `null`: the parent's fields have to be captured before the inner map shadows `$`.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
---
payload flatMap ((order) -> (order.line_items default []) map ((li) -> {
  orderId: order.order_id,
  customer: order.customer,
  sku: li.sku,
  qty: li.qty,
  price: li.price
}))

explanation.approach: The row count here is decided by the children, not the parents: one order can become zero rows, one row, or five. That rules out a plain `map`, which always produces exactly one output element per input element — the tool for `n` inputs to a variable number of outputs is `flatMap`, which runs a function that itself returns an array for each element, then concatenates all of those arrays into one flat list. Inside that function, the order's own fields — `order_id`, `customer` — have to be read off a named parameter, because the inner `map` over `line_items` rebinds `$` to the line item; reaching for `$.order_id` there silently reads a field that does not exist on a line item and gets `null` instead of an error.

snippets.label: map alone gives one array per order, not one flat list
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map ((order) -> order.line_items map ((li) -> { orderId: order.order_id, sku: li.sku }))
snippets.note: Two orders in, two arrays out — nested one level too deep for a flat CSV, where every line item needs to be a sibling row, not tucked inside its parent's array.

snippets.label: flatMap flattens that one level, which is exactly one level too many
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---

snippets.note: Same shape of function, but flattened into one list of rows, `orderId` repeated on each one — this is the sibling-rows shape the CSV writer needs.

title: Rows into columns, columns unknown in advance
prompt:
You are given exam records, each `{ student, subject, score }` — one row per student per subject they sat. Pivot this into one CSV row per student, with one column per subject.

The list of subjects is not given anywhere; it has to be discovered from the data, in the order each subject first appears. If a student has no record for some subject that other students do have, that student's cell for it is `0` — every row must have every column, or the file is not a rectangle.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
---
hints: The columns aren't a fixed list you can type into the script — they have to be read off the data itself, once, before you build a single row. Get that list first; building it row by row as you go is how two students end up with columns in a different order.

`groupBy` gets you one bucket of records per student. For each bucket, don't just turn the records you have into columns — walk the full discovered list of subjects and look up a score for each one, so a student misses a subject rather than the subject disappearing from their row.

`(payload map $.subject) distinctBy $` gives the subjects in first-seen order — `distinctBy` keeps the first match, so that order is stable no matter which student saw a subject first. Then `reduce` over that same list, once per student, building `{ student: ... }` up one column at a time, defaulting a missing lookup to `0` rather than leaving the key out.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
var subjects = (payload map $.subject) distinctBy $
---
payload groupBy $.student pluck ((rows, student) -> subjects reduce ((subj, acc = { student: student }) -> acc ++ { (subj): (rows filter ($.subject == subj))[0].score default 0 }))

explanation.approach: The set of output columns is not known until the whole input has been looked at, so it has to be computed once, up front, rather than assembled row by row. `(payload map $.subject) distinctBy $` collects every subject exactly once, in the order it first shows up, and `distinctBy` keeping the first match is what makes that order the same regardless of which student happens to mention a subject first. From there, `groupBy $.student` buckets the records per student, and for each bucket a `reduce` over the full subject list — not over that student's own rows — builds one row with a key for every column, filling in `0` wherever that student has no matching record. Reducing over the student's own rows instead of the discovered list is the natural-looking mistake: it works until two students have different subjects, at which point the rows stop having the same columns.

output application/json
---
(payload map $.subject) distinctBy $
snippets.note: Math and Bio, each once, in the order they first appear — Bo's second Math record does not add a duplicate or move anything.

---

title: Validate a record against a schema given as data
prompt:
The payload is `{ schema, record }`. `schema` is an object mapping field names to a rule shaped like `{ kind, required }`, where `kind` is one of `"String"`, `"Number"`, `"Boolean"`, `"Object"`, `"Array"`, and `required` is `true` or `false`.

When `kind` is `"Object"`, the rule also has `fields` — another schema of the same shape, describing `record`'s nested value for that field. When `kind` is `"Array"`, the rule also has `itemKind` — one of the scalar kinds, which every element of the array must match.

Return an array of every violation found anywhere in `record`, as strings, in the form `<path> is required` or `<path> must be a <Kind>`, using a dotted path such as `user.address.city` and a bracketed index such as `tags[1]` for array elements. A field that is missing is only a violation when its rule says it is required. Find every violation, not just the first one for a field and not just the first field with a problem — a record with three things wrong reports all three.
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun validate(path, schema, record) =
  ???
---
validate("", payload.schema, payload.record)

cases.output: ["name is required", "age must be a Number"]
["tags[1] must be a String", "tags[3] must be a String"]
["order.id is required", "order.tags[1] must be a String"]

hints: For each field the schema mentions, look up the matching value in the record and ask the same two questions: is it missing when it shouldn't be, and if it's present, does it have the shape the rule describes. That question is identical at every depth — the only thing that changes going into a nested Object field is which schema and which value you're asking it about.

Each field resolves to its own small array of errors — often empty. The overall answer is every one of those little arrays, flattened into one, which is a job for `pluck` (it hands you the rule and the field name for every entry) rather than a variable you keep appending to as you go.

`match` on `rule.kind` picks the check. `"Object"` and `"Array"` are not leaves: for `"Object"`, call the validator again on `rule.fields` and the nested value, with the path extended by the field's name; for `"Array"`, check `rule.itemKind` against every element and collect all of their errors. A version that only confirms the value IS an Object, or IS an Array, without going one level further in, matches a flat schema exactly and reports nothing at all for anything nested inside one.

explanation.approach: Each field in the schema resolves to its own small array of errors — empty when that field is fine — and the overall result is every one of those arrays flattened together, so nothing needs a running total that grows as the walk proceeds. `pluck` supplies the `(rule, field)` pairs; for each one, `record[field]` is looked up and tested for missing-when-required, then, if it is present, matched against `rule.kind`. Three of the five kinds are leaves and get checked with `is` directly. The other two are not: `"Object"` means there is a nested schema (`rule.fields`) and a nested value, and `validate` is called again on exactly those, with the path extended by the field's own name; `"Array"` means every element gets checked against `rule.itemKind` and all of those results get flattened in too. The near-miss stops at confirming the field's own container type and never goes back inside it — which behaves identically to the real thing on a schema that happens not to nest, and silently drops every violation that lives one level deeper.

snippets.note: Two independent problems on two independent fields, both present in the result — neither one stops the walk before the other is found.

snippets.label: An empty schema has nothing to check
snippets.note: `pluck` over an empty object produces nothing to flatten, whatever the record itself contains — there is no rule to hold it to.

snippets.label: Errors from two different nested branches both survive
snippets.note: `user.name` is missing and `user.address.city` is missing two levels down — both come back, with the path built up one field at a time as `validate` calls itself.

snippets.label: The near-miss on that same nested payload: silence
snippets.note: `user` is present and is an Object, so `check` says it's fine and stops — `rule.fields` is never looked at, so the two missing fields inside it are never found.

snippets.label: The same near-miss still catches a top-level type mismatch
snippets.note: This is why the bug ships unnoticed: it is not silent about everything, only about what is nested. A field of the wrong container type at the top level is still caught; it is only the contents of a correctly-typed Object or Array that never get looked at.

snippets.label: Every bad element of an array is reported, not just the first

expect.output: ["tags[1] must be a String", "tags[3] must be a String"]

snippets.note: Index `1` (the number) and index `3` (the boolean) are both wrong, and both come back — `map` runs `check` against every element independently before the results are flattened together.
